title: Ajamila's last word: the name at the end
hookLine: dying and afraid, Ajamila calls his son's name, Narayana, and the Lord's messengers come; the Isha's last verses ask the mind to remember
carry: smarana: keep the lord's name close
last: DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.

cards: An old man is dying, and he's afraid. He's eighty-eight, and he has spent most of his life gambling, cheating and stealing to keep his family fed.
Now he sees three terrible figures with ropes, the messengers of Yama, lord of death, come to drag him away. His youngest son is playing a little way off. The old man calls out to him by name.
And the boy's name is Narayana.

teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its sixth book. Ajamila had once been a careful young brahmin, before he fell into a very different life.
But Narayana is also a name of Vishnu, and when he cries it out, Vishnu's own messengers appear and stop Yama's.

teach.h: THE NAME REACHES FURTHER THAN WRONGS.
teach.b: An argument follows about dharma and deeds, and Vishnu's messengers win it: the Lord's name, said even to call a child, even without meaning it, reaches further than a lifetime of wrongs. Ajamila is given more life.
He goes to the Ganges at Haridwar, gives himself to devotion, and at the end goes with the Lord's messengers.
Now set beside him the Isha Upanishad's last verses, which Shankara hears as the words of someone at the end of life. Let the breath go to the wind; let this body end in ashes. Then: Om.

teach.h: OM. MIND, REMEMBER WHAT WAS DONE.
teach.b: Remember what was done. Said twice. The last verse asks Agni, the fire, to lead by a good path; it also appears in the Rig Veda.

Two Hindu answers to the last moment, and they meet. The Isha, as many read it, asks for an honest look at your karma, everything you did. The Bhagavata says the Lord's name can carry you further still.

That's the teaching of smarana, remembering: keep the Lord's name close every day, so it's what the mind reaches for when it matters. Krishna says it in the Gita: whoever leaves the body remembering me comes to me.
It's why families chant the name beside someone who is dying, and why some people say Ram, Ram, every night before sleep.

how: Many Hindu families chant the Lord's name, or play recitations, beside someone who is dying, and in many North Indian funeral processions mourners call 'Ram naam satya hai', the name of Ram is truth. Many keep the name close every day through japa.

o: luck: the good or bad that simply happens to you
the deeds of a life, which the Isha says to remember
a prayer asking the sun to lift a golden lid

games.q: the name and the last verses — tap the pairs.
p: calls his son's name at death
asked to lead by a good path

s: Ajamila is saved because he lived a careful life
he had fallen far; the Lord's name, called even for his son, reached further.
the Isha's last verse is addressed to Agni, the fire
it asks the fire to lead by a good path; the same verse appears in the Rig Veda.
at its end the Isha asks the mind to forget everything
it says the opposite, twice: mind, remember what was done.

games.q: you're one of Vishnu's messengers. Ajamila's life was full of wrongs, but he called 'Narayana' at the end. Yama's messengers want him. what do you say?
o: take him: his deeds decide everything.
stop: the Lord's name, even said for a son, reaches further.
let him pick a new life.
games.why: in the Bhagavata, Vishnu's messengers stop Yama's: the name reaches further than a lifetime of wrongs. Ajamila lives, and turns to devotion.

practice: If you pray, choose one name of God, the one your family uses, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, and say it slowly, once with each breath, ten times. If you don't, choose a word that holds what you love most.
Then do what the Isha asks, gently: remember what was done today, without grading any of it. End with the name once more.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, everything a person did. At the end, the Isha asks the mind to remember it; the Bhagavata says the Lord's name reaches further still.

orig.note: Sanskrit kṛtam, what was done (Isha 17: kṛtaṃ smara, remember what was done); from kṛ, to do, the root of karma too.

carryVoice: Your line: smarana, keep the Lord's name close. Tomorrow, a servant's boy who heard the stories and fell in love. Day six hundred ninety-two, done.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 17 (oṃ krato smara, kṛtaṃ smara)
